title: High Performers Must Manage the Expectations of Others or Be Judged Unfairly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues top performers are judged more harshly than others precisely because their past success raises the baseline expectation for everything they do next. The author's proposed remedy isn't lowering the bar but making the process behind performance visible -- 'showing their work' the way a math student shows steps -- so others can evaluate the decisions and choices behind an outcome, not just the outcome itself. This reframes fair judgment as something high performers must actively construct for others rather than something owed to them automatically.
points: Because past excellence sets a higher baseline, high performers face harsher judgment on any performance that merely looks average.
The fix isn't lowering expectations but making the process behind performance visible, so others can judge decisions and steps, not just outcomes.
A worked example: a negotiator who falls short can still point to a well-crafted opening position or a well-timed trade-off as genuine progress.
The burden of fair judgment is reframed as something high performers must actively create for others, not something owed to them by default.
quotes: The performance of top talent is judged more harshly than that of others.

For high performers, the game of managing expectations isn’t about lowering the bar — it’s about clarifying what they do, how they do it, and asking people to judge them on the process, not the results.
They don’t let others judge them on results alone. They insist on being evaluated for the process and decisions behind those results.

By making their performance process visible to others and highlighting any progress made, regardless of outcome, they teach others to judge them more fairly and not to treat every outcome as a win or loss.
Ultimately, the burden of fair judgment falls not on the observer but on the high performers themselves.
